1.o: The book begins with the history, not of Joshua's life (many remarkable passages of that we had before in the books of Moses) but of his reign and government. In this chapter, I. God appoints him to the government in the stead of Moses, gives him an ample commission, full instructions, and great encouragements, ver. 1-9. II. He accepts the government, and addresses himself immediately to the business of it, giving orders to the officers of the people in general, ver.
1.i: After Moses died, God told Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan, promising to be with him as He had been with Moses, and told him three times to be strong and courageous.
1.p: Lord, be with us as You were with Joshua. Make us strong and courageous, and help us to keep Your word on our lips. Amen.
1.l: Say this to yourself today whenever you feel nervous: Be strong and courageous. The Lord my God is with me.
q: God's reason for courage was that He would be with Joshua. What are you waiting to feel before you act?

2.o: In this chapter we have an account of the scouts that were employed to bring an account to Joshua of the posture of the city of Jericho. Observe here, I. How Joshua sent them, ver. 1. II. How Rahab received them, and protected them, and told a lie for them (ver. 2-7), so that they escaped out of the hands of the enemy. III. The account she gave them of the present posture of Jericho, and the panic-fear they were struck with upon the approach of Israel, ver. 8-11. IV.
2.i: Rahab of Jericho hid Joshua's two spies, confessed that the Lord is God of heaven and earth, and was promised safety for her family by a scarlet cord in her window.
2.p: Lord, thank You for saving those who trust You, whoever they are. Make us brave, like Rahab. Amen.
2.l: Do one brave kind thing today for someone who needs it, even if it is a little scary.
q: Rahab acted on what she had heard about God. What have you heard about Him that you could act on?

3.o: This chapter, and that which follows it, give us the history of Israel's passing through Jordan into Canaan, and a very memorable history it is. Long afterwards, they are told to remember what God did for them between Shittim (whence they decamped, ver. 1) and Gilgal, where they next pitched, ch. iv. 19, Mic. vi. 5, that they might know the righteousness of the Lord. By Joshua's order they marched up to the river's side, (ver. 1), and then almighty power led them through it.
3.i: Joshua 3 shows the careful preparation before Israel crossed the Jordan, and the promise that God would lead them where they had never been.
3.p: Lord, You lead us where we have never been. Help us to follow, one step at a time, trusting that You go before us. Amen.
3.l: When you do not know the way forward, take the next step you do know, and ask God to show you the rest.
q: Joshua rose early to set an example. What small habit of yours would you want others to copy?

4.o: This chapter gives a further account of the miraculous passage of Israel through Jordan. I. The provision that was made at that time to preserve the memorial of it, by twelve stones set up in Jordan (ver. 9) and other twelve stones taken up out of Jordan, ver. 1-8. II. The march of the people through Jordan's channel, the two tribes first, then all the people, and the priests that bore the ark last, ver. 10-14. III. The closing of the waters again upon their coming up with the ark, ver. 15-19. IV.
4.i: After crossing the Jordan, twelve men carried twelve stones from the riverbed to Gilgal as a memorial to teach future generations what God had done.
4.p: Lord, You do great things so we will remember. Help us to tell our children the stories of Your goodness. Amen.
4.l: Find a stone or other small object that reminds you of something God did for you. Tell someone the story.
q: The same site served for crossings, kings and returns. What place in your life has been the start of several chapters?

5.o: Israel have now got over Jordan, and the waters which had opened before them, to favour their march forward, are closed again behind them, to forbid their retreat backward. They have now got footing in Canaan, and must apply themselves to the conquest of it, in order to which this chapter tells us, I. How their enemies were dispirited, ver. 1. II. What was done at their first landing to assist and encourage them. 1. The covenant of circumcision was renewed, ver. 2-9. 2.
5.i: Joshua 5 marks a turning point at Gilgal: the manna ends, the Passover is kept, and Joshua meets a visitor who will not take sides.
5.p: Lord, You command the armies of heaven. Teach us to follow You, and to stand on holy ground with humble hearts. Amen.
5.l: Before you decide something today, stop for a moment and ask God what He wants.
q: How would your day change if you asked whose side you are on before asking whose side God is on?

6.o: Joshua opened the campaign with the siege of Jericho, a city which could not trust so much to the courage of its people as to act offensively, and to send out its forces to oppose Israel's landing and encamping, but trusted so much to the strength of its walls as to stand upon its defence, and not to surrender, or desire conditions of peace. Now here we have the story of the taking of it, I. The directions and assurances which the captain of the Lord's host gave concerning it, ver. 1-5. II.
6.i: Joshua 6:1-14 slows down for the days before the walls fell, and shows what it looks like to obey when nothing seems to happen.
6.p: Lord, You keep Your promises before we see them. Give us patience to keep obeying when nothing seems to change. Amen.
6.l: Keep doing one good habit today, like reading or praying, even if you do not feel anything change yet.
q: What are you doing faithfully right now without seeing any results?

7.o: More than once we have found the affairs of Israel, even when they were in the happiest posture and gave the most hopeful prospects, perplexed and embarrassed by sin, and a stop thereby put to the most promising proceedings. The golden calf, the murmuring at Kadesh, and the iniquity of Peor, had broken their measures and given them great disturbance; and in this chapter we have such another instance of the interruption given to the progress of their arms by sin.
7.i: Achan's secret theft at Jericho led to Israel's defeat at Ai, and showed that hidden sin harms everyone.
7.p: Lord, search our hearts and show us what we hide. Forgive us, and turn our valleys of trouble into doors of hope. Amen.
7.l: If there is something you have been keeping secret that you should not, tell a trusted grown-up today.
q: Achan's hidden sin hurt a whole nation. What hidden thing in your life might be hurting people you love?

8.o: The embarrassment which Achan's sin gave to the affairs of Israel being over, we have them here in a very good posture again, the affairs both of war and religion. Here is, I. The glorious progress of their arms in the taking of Ai, before which they had lately suffered disgrace. 1. God encourages Joshua to attack it, with the assurance of success, and directs him what method to take, ver. 1, 2. 2. Joshua gives orders accordingly to the men of war, ver. 3-8. 3.
8.i: After the first victories in the land, Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal, wrote the law on stones, and read all of it, blessings and curses, to every man, woman and child.
8.p: Lord, thank You for Your Word. Help us to hear it, obey it, and say Amen with our whole lives. Amen.
8.l: Read one short Bible passage out loud to someone today.
q: All the people heard every word, and said Amen. How well do you listen when God's Word is read?

9.o: Here is in this chapter, I. The impolite confederacy of the kings of Canaan against Israel, ver. 1, 2. II. The polite confederacy of the inhabitants of Gibeon with Israel, 1. How it was subtly proposed and petitioned for by the Gibeonites pretending to come from a far country, ver. 3-13. 2. How it was unwarily consented to by Joshua and the Israelites, to the disgust of the congregation when the fraud was discovered, ver. 14-18. 3.
9.i: Joshua 9 tells how a clever delegation tricked Israel into a treaty, and how Israel kept the oath anyway.
9.p: Lord, give us wisdom to ask You before we decide, and faithfulness to keep our word. Amen.
9.l: Keep a promise today that is a little hard to keep, and ask God before you make the next one.
q: Is there a decision you should pray about before you make it?

10.o: We have in this chapter an account of the conquest of the kings and kingdoms of the southern part of the land of Canaan, as, in the next chapter, of the reduction of the northern parts, which together completed the glorious successes of the wars of Canaan. In this chapter we have an account, I. Of the routing of their forces in the field, in which observe, 1. Their confederacy against the Gibeonites, ver. 1-5. 2. The Gibeonites' request to Joshua to assist them, ver. 6. 3.
10.i: When five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, Joshua marched all night, God sent hailstones, and Joshua prayed that the sun and moon would stand still until the victory was won.
10.p: Lord, You hear the prayers of faith. Give us courage to ask great things of You, and to trust You for the answer. Amen.
10.l: Pray a big prayer today for something you cannot do yourself, and believe that God can answer.
q: Joshua asked for something big, and God did it. What big prayer have you been afraid to pray?

11.o: This chapter continues and concludes the history of the conquest of Canaan; of the reduction of the southern parts we had an account in the foregoing chapter, after which we may suppose Joshua allowed his forces some breathing-time; now here we have the story of the war in the north, and the happy success of that war. I. The confederacy of the northern crowns against Israel, ver. 1-5. II. The encouragement which God gave to Joshua to engage them, ver. 6. III. His victory over them, ver. 7-9. IV.
11.i: Joshua 11 is the last great battle of the conquest, against a coalition of northern kings led by Hazor.
11.p: Lord, You fight for Your people. Teach us to trust You more than our own strength, and to obey You in every detail. Amen.
11.l: When you feel outnumbered today, say a short prayer: Lord, You are with me.
q: Israel should see chariots as rotten wood. What do you trust in that looks strong and is not?

12.o: This chapter is a summary of Israel's conquests. I. Their conquests under Moses, on the other side Jordan (for we now suppose ourselves in Canaan) eastward, which we had the history of, Num. xxi. 24, &c. And here the abridgment of that history, ver. 1-6. II. Their conquests under Joshua, on this side Jordan, westward. 1. The country they reduced, ver. 7, 8. 2. The kings they subdued, thirty-one in all, ver. 9-24.

13.o: At this chapter begins the account of the dividing of the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel by lot, a narrative not so entertaining and instructive as that of the conquest of it, and yet it is thought fit to be inserted in the sacred history, to illustrate the performance of the promise made to the fathers, that this land should be given to the seed of Jacob, to them and not to any other.
13.i: Joshua 13 to 16 look like a list of place names, but each name is a family's home, given by lot.
13.p: Lord, You give each family a place. Thank You for our homes, and give us courage to finish what You start in us. Amen.
13.l: Thank God today for your home and the people who share it with you.
q: The lot-holders fell short from sluggishness and unbelief. What did you start well and leave unfinished?

14.o: Here is, I. The general method that was taken in dividing the land, ver. 1-5. II. The demand Caleb made of Hebron, as his by promise, and therefore not to be put into the lot with the rest, ver. 6-12. And Joshua's grant of that demand, ver. 13-15. This was done at Gilgal, which was as yet their head-quarters.
14.i: At eighty-five, Caleb asks Joshua for the hill country of Hebron, where the giants live, because God promised it.
14.p: Lord, give us hearts like Caleb's, ready to follow You wholly. Amen.
14.l: Choose the harder job today when you have a choice, and ask God to help you finish it.
q: Caleb asked for the hardest place at eighty-five. What big thing do you still want to ask God for?

15.o: Though the land was not completely conquered, yet being (as was said in the close of the foregoing chapter) as rest from war for the present, and their armies all drawn out of the field to a general rendezvous at Gilgal, there they began to divide the land, though the work was afterwards perfected at Shiloh, ch. xviii. 1, &c. In this chapter we have the lot of the tribe of Judah, which in this, as in other things, had the precedency. I. The borders or bounds of the inheritance of Judah, ver. 1-12. II.
15.i: Joshua 13 to 16 look like a list of place names, but each name is a family's home, given by lot.
15.p: Lord, You give each family a place. Thank You for our homes, and give us courage to finish what You start in us. Amen.
15.l: Thank God today for your home and the people who share it with you.
q: The lot-holders fell short from sluggishness and unbelief. What did you start well and leave unfinished?

16.o: It is a pity that this and the following chapter should be separated, for both of them give us the lot of the children of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, who, next to Judah, were to have the post of honour, and therefore had the first and best portion in the northern part of Canaan, as Judah now had in the southern part. In this chapter we have, I. A general account of the lot of these two tribes together, ver. 1-4. II. The borders of the lot of Ephraim in particular, ver. 5-10.
16.i: Joshua 13 to 16 look like a list of place names, but each name is a family's home, given by lot.
16.p: Lord, You give each family a place. Thank You for our homes, and give us courage to finish what You start in us. Amen.
16.l: Thank God today for your home and the people who share it with you.
q: The lot-holders fell short from sluggishness and unbelief. What did you start well and leave unfinished?

17.o: The half tribe of Manasseh comes next to be provided for; and here we have, I. The families of that tribe that were to be portioned, ver. 1-6. II. The country that fell to their lot, ver. 7-13. III. The joint request of the two tribes that descended from Joseph, for the enlargement of their lot, and Joshua's answer to that request, ver. 14-18.
17.i: When the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh complained of too little land, Joshua told them to clear the forest themselves, and to trust God to help them drive out their enemies.
17.p: Lord, thank You for the gifts You give and the work You have for us. Make us willing workers and not complainers. Amen.
17.l: Do one job today that you have been putting off, and finish it. Notice how it feels.
q: The people asked for more land but did not want the work. Where are you waiting for a gift that needs your effort?

18.o: In this chapter we have, I. The setting up of the tabernacle at Shiloh, ver. 1. II. The stirring up of the seven tribes that were yet unsettled to look after their lot, and the putting of them in a method for it, by Joshua, ver. 2-7. III. The distributing of the land into seven lots, by certain men employed for that purpose, ver. 8, 9. IV. The determining of these seven portions to the seven tribes yet unprovided for by lot, ver. 10. V. The particular lot of the tribe of Benjamin, the borders of it, ver. 11-20.
18.i: With seven tribes still without land, Joshua sent twenty-one men to survey and describe it, then drew lots at Shiloh before the Lord to give each tribe its share.
18.p: Lord, You give each of us a place. Help us not to delay in taking up what You have prepared. Amen.
18.l: Draw a map of your neighborhood today, with your house, your friends' houses, and a place where you feel safe.
q: Seven tribes waited to take their land. What blessing are you waiting to claim?

19.o: In the description of the lots of Judah and Benjamin we have an account both of the borders that surrounded them and of the cities contained in them. In that of Ephraim and Manasseh we have the borders, but not the cities; in this chapter Simeon and Dan are described by their cities only, and not their borders, because they lay very much within Judah, especially the former; the rest have both their borders described and their cities names, especially frontiers. Here is, I. The lot of Simeon, ver. 1-9. II.
19.i: After the land is divided, Joshua is given the town he requested, Timnath-serah, and settles in it.
19.p: Lord, You give rest to Your people. Keep us humble, and let us be glad to take the last place. Amen.
19.l: Let someone else go first today, and take the last place gladly.
q: Joshua took his own share last. When do you put others first?

20.o: This short chapter is concerning the cities of refuge, which we often read of in the writings of Moses, but this is the last time that we find mention of them, for now that matter was thoroughly settled. Here is, I. The law God gave concerning them, ver. 1-6. II. The people's designation of the particular cities for that use, ver. 7-9. And this remedial law was a figure of good things to come.
20.i: Joshua 20 sets apart six towns where someone who caused a death by accident could run and be safe until the matter was judged.
20.p: Lord, You are a refuge for the weary and the guilty. Make us a refuge for others, and teach us justice and mercy. Amen.
20.l: Be a safe person today: when someone makes a mistake, help them instead of blaming them.
q: God appointed refuges as soon as he gave rest. Who in your community needs a place to run to without being asked questions first?

21.o: It had been often said that the tribe of Levi should have "no inheritance with their brethren," no particular part of the country assigned them, as the other tribes had, no, not the country about Shiloh, which one might have expected to be appropriated to them as the lands of the church; but, though they were not thus cast into a country by themselves, it appears, by the provision made for them in this chapter, that they were no losers, but the rest of the tribes were very much gainers, by their being dispersed.
21.i: After the land is divided, Joshua is given the town he requested, Timnath-serah, and settles in it.
21.p: Lord, You give rest to Your people. Keep us humble, and let us be glad to take the last place. Amen.
21.l: Let someone else go first today, and take the last place gladly.
q: Joshua took his own share last. When do you put others first?

22.o: Many particular things we have read concerning the two tribes and a half, though nothing separated them from the rest of the tribes except the river Jordan, and this chapter is wholly concerning them. I. Joshua's dismission of the militia of those tribes from the camp of Israel, in which the had served as auxiliaries, during all the wars of Canaan, and their return thereupon to their own country, ver. 1-9. II. The altar they built on the borders of Jordan, in token of their communion with the land of Israel, ver.
22.i: Israel nearly went to war over a misunderstanding about an altar, but a visit and an honest conversation proved it was a witness, not a rival.
22.p: Lord, make us slow to anger and quick to listen. Keep us from wars we do not need to fight. Amen.
22.l: Next time you hear something upsetting about a friend, ask them about it before you decide it is true.
q: The tribes asked before they fought. Who needs a question from you before you assume the worst?

23.o: In this and the following chapter we have two farewell sermons, which Joshua preached to the people of Israel a little before his death. Had he designed to gratify the curiosity of succeeding ages, he would rather have recorded the method of Israel's settlement in their new conquests, their husbandry, manufacturers, trade, customs, courts of justice, and the constitutions of their infant commonwealth, which one would wish to be informed of; but that which he intended in the registers of this book was to entail on…
23.i: The aged Joshua tells Israel that the Lord has kept every promise and urges them to stay faithful.
23.p: Lord, You keep every promise. Help us to love You and be faithful to You all our days. Amen.
23.l: Think of one promise God made that came true in your life, and thank Him for it.
q: Joshua said not one promise failed. What promises of God do you hold on to?

24.o: This chapter concludes the life and reign of Joshua, in which we have, I. The great care and pains he took to confirm the people of Israel in the true faith and worship of God, that they might, after his death, persevere therein. In order to this he called another general assembly of the heads of the congregation of Israel (ver. 1) and dealt with them. 1. By way of narrative, recounting the great things God had done for them and their fathers, ver. 2-13. 2.
24.s: As for Me and My House
24.i: At Shechem the old leader Joshua reminded Israel of all God had done and challenged them to choose whom they would serve, declaring that he and his family would serve the Lord.
24.p: Lord, we choose You. Help our families to serve You faithfully, today and always. Amen.
24.l: Say out loud or write down: this is what my family will serve. Then do one thing to show it.
q: Joshua said as for me and my house. What does your household serve, in practice?
